pl-l4d17c3-d1e112.summary: States that one must confess to priests, as is proved not only by James, 'confess your sins to one another', but by many other testimonies.

pl-l4d17c3-d1e118.summary: Quotes Augustine: let a man judge himself willingly while he can and amend his ways, lest he be judged against his will; and having passed sentence on himself, come to the bishops through whom the keys are ministered, and receive from them the measure of satisfaction, offering a contrite heart. If his sin causes great scandal and the bishop judges it useful, let him not refuse public penance. When the wound of sin is so great that the medicine of the Lord's body must be deferred, he should withdraw from the altar by the bishop's authority and be reconciled by it.
claims: The penitent receives the measure of satisfaction from the bishops who hold the keys.
Public penance may be imposed for scandalous sins.
Grave sinners abstain from the altar until reconciled.

pl-l4d17c3-d1e130.summary: Quotes Leo: God's manifold mercy so helps human lapses that hope of life is restored not only by baptism but by penance, ordered so that God's indulgence cannot be obtained except through the supplications of priests; Christ gave the Church's leaders power to give satisfaction to those who confess and to readmit them, purged, to the sacraments through the door of reconciliation.
claims: Pardon is obtained through priestly supplication.
Christ gave priests power to impose satisfaction and reconcile.

pl-l4d17c3-d1e136.summary: Quotes Augustine: let the penitent present his life to God through the priest and anticipate God's judgment by confession; the Lord commanded the lepers to show themselves to priests in person, not through a messenger or in writing; the shame itself has part in remission; by confessing to the priest and overcoming shame, the crime is pardoned, and what was mortal becomes venial. God, merciful and just, judges one worthy of mercy who seeks grace by spiritual labor, and shame is a great penalty; the more one confesses, the more easily he gains remission.
claims: Confession should be in person, not in writing.
The shame of confession is part of satisfaction.

pl-l4d17c3-d1e146.summary: Quotes Leo: though faith that does not fear shame before men is praiseworthy, not all sins are such that penitents need not fear publishing them; so the improper custom of public reading should be removed, lest many be kept from penance by shame or fear of enemies and the law. Confession offered first to God, then to the priest who intercedes, suffices; more will be drawn to penance if the conscience of the confessor is not published to the people.
claims: Confessions should not be made public.
Confession to God and the priest suffices.

pl-l4d17c3-d1e152.summary: Concludes that these texts show beyond doubt that confession must be offered first to God and then to the priest, and that otherwise, if possible, one cannot reach the entrance of paradise.
claims: Confession is to God first, then to the priest, when possible.

pl-l4d17c3.summary: Proves that one must confess to priests, from James ('confess your sins to one another') and other authorities. Augustine: let a man judge himself while he can, then come to the bishops through whom the keys are ministered and receive from them the measure of satisfaction, doing public penance if the bishop judges it useful for scandal, and abstaining from the altar for grave sins until reconciled. Leo: God's mercy is so ordered that pardon cannot be obtained without the priests' supplications, Christ having given them power to impose satisfaction and readmit to communion. Augustine: present your life to God through the priest, confess in person, not in writing, since the shame itself is part of remission and makes mortal sin venial; the more one confesses, the more easily one is pardoned. Leo forbids requiring public reading of confessions; confession first to God and then to the priest suffices. So confession must be made first to God and then to the priest, if possible.
claims: Confession must be made to priests.
Priests hold the keys and impose satisfaction.
Pardon is ordinarily obtained through priestly intercession.
Confession should be in person; its shame is part of satisfaction.
Confession need not be made public.
Confession is to God first, then to the priest, if possible.
